title: A run of one character is one giant tie run under the key sort
body:
Every suffix inside a run of one character has the same key: 21 of that character for DNA. Under the key sort such a run is one tie run of as many suffixes as the run is long, and `UnmaskedKeys::order_ties` hands it to `merge_sort`, which compares text the length of the run. The LCP cache cannot help there, since inside one run every distance occurs.

A DNA build indexes only suffixes that start with A, C, G, T or the sentinel since `3944856`, so a run of N no longer forms a tie run there. A run of one base still does, and so does a run of N in a build over the byte alphabet, such as the `long-n` row of the benchmark suite.

At `276640b`, with 32 threads, hg38 with its Ns took 98.6 s against 44.1 s for hg38 with the Ns deleted, and libsais took 79.6 s on both. That build indexed the suffixes inside N runs. Nobody has measured the cost of runs since.

## Proposal

Order a tie run whose key is one repeated character from positions alone. Inside one run of character c that ends before character d, each suffix is a tail of the run followed by d:

- If d sorts after c, the longer tail sorts first, so positions go in increasing order.
- If d sorts before c, the shorter tail sorts first, so positions go in decreasing order.

Two neighbours from the same run share the length of the shorter tail. A tie run also holds suffixes from other runs of c with the same key, and the merge still orders those, once per run rather than once per suffix.

## Open

- How much time such runs cost on real genomes, now that DNA builds skip N.
